45-009.r: A true: most vitamins are not made in the body (essential food factors). R false. Gut bacteria make vitamin K and biotin; skin makes vitamin D in UV light.

45-010.r: A false: the body cannot make most vitamins. R true: vitamins are essential for proper growth; their deficiency causes specific diseases.

45-011.r: Liver stores fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K and vitamin B (not C) → none of the given options fits.

45-012.r: Fat-soluble vitamins → A, D, E, K; water-soluble → B group and C. So 'vitamin K is water-soluble' is the wrong statement.

45-020.r: Micro-minerals (trace elements, under 0.01% of body weight) → iodine, iron, zinc, copper, selenium etc.; not phosphorus, sulphur or magnesium.

45-021.r: Needed in major quantities (macronutrients) → potassium, sodium, magnesium, calcium (also sulphur, phosphorus, chlorine).

45-022.r: In a 70 kg man, increasing amount: copper < iron < sodium < potassium.

45-023.r: Apples → rich in potassium, which keeps a healthy heart rhythm; also antioxidant phytochemicals.

45-024.r: Antioxidants → neutralise free radicals produced in metabolism, stopping chain reactions that damage or kill cells.

45-026.r: Most vitamin C among chilli, pumpkin, pea and radish → chilli (about 143.7 mg per 100 g).

45-027.r: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) → citrus fruits (lemon, orange, amla); water-soluble, keeps skin healthy; deficiency → scurvy.

45-028.r: Main source of vitamin C → raw, fresh (citrus) fruits; milk and ghee give vitamin A; pulses give protein.

45-029.r: Richest vitamin C (ascorbic acid) source → Indian gooseberry (amla); orange, tomato, lemon, papaya, peas are also good sources.

45-035.r: Vitamin C → helps iron absorption; vitamin D → helps calcium and magnesium absorption.

45-036.r: Vitamin C → water-soluble, not stored (lost in urine); vitamins A, D, E, K are fat-soluble and stored (mainly in the liver).

45-037.r: Vitamin K → blood clotting (antihaemorrhagic factor); deficiency → slow coagulation and uncontrolled bleeding.

45-043.r: Antidote to anticoagulant poisons → vitamin K (antihaemorrhagic factor).

45-044.r: Made by intestinal bacteria → vitamin B and vitamin K; the book accepts both (a) and (c).

45-045.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin K – sterility; vitamin K lack affects blood clotting. Correct: niacin–pellagra, thiamin–beri-beri, vitamin D–rickets.

45-046.r: Vitamin D → made in skin by sun rays (also butter, egg yolk, liver); lack → rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults), osteoporosis (older adults).

45-050.r: Vitamin D → calciferol: D₂ ergocalciferol, D₃ cholecalciferol. Ascorbic acid = C; retinol = A; folic acid = a B vitamin.

45-053.r: Vitamin D → considered a hormone; D₂ and D₃ become active only after change in the body, to calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D).

45-054.r: Night blindness → vitamin A lack; the retina uses retinol + opsin to make rhodopsin for low-light vision.

45-055.r: Vitamin A (retinol) → stored mainly in the liver; its lack causes night blindness.

45-057.r: Carrot → richest vitamin A source among cabbage, carrot, cauliflower, spinach; spinach is rich in iron.

45-058.r: Mango → richest vitamin A source among apple, papaya, guava, mango; also rich in vitamins C and E.

45-059.r: Vitamin A → cannot be made in the human body (proteins, enzymes and hormones are).

45-060.r: Normal vision → retinol (vitamin A), part of rhodopsin, the light-absorbing protein of the retina's receptors.

45-061.r: A false: vitamin A also comes from other foods, so stopping green vegetables need not cause night blindness. R true: night blindness follows vitamin A lack.

45-062.r: Cobalt → found in vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin), a water-soluble vitamin; its lack causes pernicious anaemia.

45-065.r: Vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin) → water-soluble yet stored in the liver for about 3-5 years: A and R both true, R not the explanation.

45-066.r: Cyanocobalamin → manufactured form of vitamin B₁₂, used to treat B₁₂ deficiency.

45-067.r: Thiamine → vitamin B₁ (water-soluble; rice bran, whole wheat, yeast); its lack causes beri-beri.

45-068.r: Beri-beri → vitamin B₁ (thiamin); rickets → vitamin D; scurvy → vitamin C.

45-069.r: Vitamin B group (B vitamins, folate) → may affect dream quality and the ability to recall dreams.

45-070.r: Vitamin D–cod-liver oil, E–wheat germ oil, K–alfalfa are right; orange (rich in C) is also a low source of B → book picks (e).

45-071.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin B₂ – cod-liver oil; cod-liver oil gives omega-3, vitamins A and D. Riboflavin (B₂) → eggs, milk, green vegetables.

45-072.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin A – orange; orange is rich in vitamin C, folate, thiamin. Vitamin A sources: carrots, milk, butter, egg, cod liver oil.

45-073.r: Vitamin K → alfalfa; D → cod-liver oil; E → wheat germ oil; C → lemon.

45-074.r: Vitamin A → blindness (night blindness, xerophthalmia); B → beriberi; C → scurvy; D → rickets.

45-075.r: Night blindness → vitamin A; rickets → D; scurvy → C; beri-beri → B.

45-076.r: Rickets → vitamin D; beri-beri → B; nyctalopia (night blindness) → A; scurvy → C.

45-077.r: Vitamin C → scurvy; folic acid → anaemia; vitamin A → night blindness; vitamin B → beri-beri.

45-078.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin D – colour blindness; colour blindness is a sex-linked genetic disorder. Correct: A–night blindness, niacin (B₃)–pellagra, folic acid–anaemia.

45-079.r: Correct: vitamin C–scurvy, vitamin D–rickets. Wrong: vitamin E–night blindness (night blindness comes from vitamin A lack).

45-080.r: Riboflavin (vitamin B₂) lack → cheilosis (swollen, cracked lips) and angular stomatitis; not pellagra, scurvy or beri-beri.

45-081.r: Wrong pair: Riboflavin – beri-beri; beri-beri is from thiamin (B₁) lack. Correct: calciferol–osteomalacia, niacin–pellagra, cobalamin–pernicious anaemia.

45-082.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin A – rheumatism; vitamin A lack causes night blindness. Correct: D–rickets, C–bleeding gums, B–beriberi.

45-083.r: Retinol (A) → conjunctivitis; tocopherol (E) → sterility; cyanocobalamin (B₁₂) → pernicious anaemia; pyridoxine (B₆) → mental illness.

45-084.r: Wrong pair: Tocopherol (E) – beri-beri; beri-beri is from thiamin (B₁) lack. Correct: retinol–xerophthalmia, cyanocobalamin–anaemia, ergocalciferol–rickets.

45-085.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin D – antisterility factor; vitamin E (tocopherol) is the antisterility factor. Correct: B–antianaemic, C–antiscorbutic, K–antihaemorrhagic.

45-086.r: Wrong pair: Vitamin K – sterility; vitamin K (naphthoquinone) is antihaemorrhagic, sterility is from vitamin E lack. Correct: thiamin–beri-beri, D–rickets, niacin–pellagra.
45-086.t: Vitamin E, not K, is linked to sterility.

45-087.r: Highest vitamin E → wheat germ oil (germ is only about 2.5% of the wheat kernel); vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant.

45-088.r: Thyroxine → a hormone of the thyroid gland, not a vitamin; niacin, riboflavin and pyridoxine are B vitamins.

45-089.r: Banana (family Musaceae) gives about 89 kcal per 100 g; among the options, 116 kcal is nearest.

45-090.r: Legumes → highly nutritious as they are rich in protein; low in fat, no cholesterol; good meat substitute.

45-091.r: Highest protein → soybean (about 40% protein, 20-23% fat, 30% carbohydrate); counted as both oilseed and pulse.

45-094.r: Richest protein source among rice, groundnut, apple → groundnut; rice is best for carbohydrate.

45-095.r: Rich in both protein and fat → groundnut (about 25.3% protein, 48.1% fat).

45-096.r: Mostly carbohydrate → rice (highest carbohydrate share among wheat, barley, rice, maize).

45-097.r: Tyrosine → helps make neurotransmitters (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine), raises energy, eases stress and depression; it does not protect against ageing free radicals.

45-098.r: Bread-making quality of wheat → gluten, a protein composite that gives dough elasticity.

45-099.r: Daily energy for a man doing very hard work → about 3500-4000 kilocalories.

45-100.r: A glass of water → zero calories (no fat, carbohydrate or protein).

45-101.r: Essential constituent of diet → carbohydrate (compounds of C, H, O with two hydrogens per oxygen).

45-102.r: Main fuel during long, high-intensity exercise → carbohydrate.

45-103.r: Nitrogen → essential in DNA, RNA, proteins and chlorophyll; not in carbohydrates (only C, H, O).

45-104.r: Acid–alkali balance in the body → phosphorus (as phosphate).

45-105.r: Amino acids → not stored in the body (need daily intake); glycogen, fat and tocopherol are stored.

45-106.r: Karonda → rich source of iron (used against anaemia); also has vitamin C (antiscorbutic).

45-107.r: Muscle contraction needs calcium, iron and sodium (also magnesium, potassium) → all three.

45-108.r: Spinach → rich in iron (and calcium): about 6.43 mg iron in 180 g boiled spinach.

45-110.r: Most iron among beans, eggs, green vegetables, milk → green vegetables; iron in haemoglobin carries oxygen; its lack causes anaemia.

45-111.r: Basmati grains lengthen on cooking → high amylose, a long straight starch that does not gelatinise (the other rice starch is amylopectin).

45-112.r: Sweetness of milk → lactose, a disaccharide of glucose + galactose.

45-113.r: Milk sugar → lactose (glucose + galactose); sucrose = glucose + fructose; maltose = glucose + glucose.

45-114.r: Milk turns sour / into curd → Lactobacillus bacteria, which turn lactose into lactic acid.

45-116.r: Slightly yellow colour of cow's milk → carotene (from hay, grass, green leaves); vitamin A gives milk no colour.

45-117.r: Cow milk is yellowish-white → carotene (yellow) with casein (white, about 80% of cow-milk protein); buffalo milk is whiter, no carotene.

45-118.r: Buffalo milk fat → about 7-7.5% (answer 7.2%); cow milk fat → about 3.5-4.0%.

45-119.r: Rennin and lactase start to disappear by age two or three and vanish between 6-15 years ('lactose intolerant') → book gives no single answer (*).

45-120.r: Milk protein → digested by rennin, a stomach enzyme of young mammals that curdles milk; HCl activates it from prorenin.

45-121.r: Casein → milk protein (a phosphoprotein) that also makes milk white; other milk proteins: lactoglobulin, lactalbumin.

45-124.r: Body tissues are built by proteins (about 17% of body weight).

45-125.r: Slow growth of the body → protein deficiency (protein builds muscle, bone, skin).

45-126.r: All proteins contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (some also traces of sulphur, iodine, iron); built from amino acids.

45-127.r: Vitamin B₁₂ → cobalt; haemoglobin → iron; chlorophyll → magnesium; brass → copper.
45-127.h: Chlorophyll Mg, haemoglobin Fe, B₁₂ Co.

45-128.r: Vitamin B₁₂ → cobalt; haemoglobin → iron; chlorophyll → magnesium; chalcopyrite → copper.

45-129.r: B₁ → thiamine (printed 'Thymine'); B₂ → riboflavin; B₆ → pyridoxine; B₁₂ → cobalamin. Calciferol is vitamin D.
45-129.h: B₁ thiamin, B₂ riboflavin, B₃ niacin, B₅ pantothenic acid, B₆ pyridoxine, B₇ biotin, B₉ folic acid, B₁₂ cobalamin.
45-129.t: Thiamine (vitamin B₁) is not thymine, a DNA base.

45-131.r: Not a micronutrient → sulphur (a macronutrient); micronutrients: iron, zinc, manganese, boron, copper, molybdenum, nickel.

45-132.r: Main vitamin in papaya → vitamin C (about 226 mg in a 200 g papaya); Columbus called it 'the fruit of the angel'.

45-133.r: Not a natural vitamin A source → milk (very little vitamin A); mango, papaya and carrot are sources.

45-134.r: Infrared rays do not denature proteins; heat, X-rays and heavy-metal salts do.

45-135.r: Wrong: 'about 30% of body weight is protein' – NCERT says about 20%. True: proteins come from animals and plants, are made of amino acids, are building blocks.

45-136.r: Protein requirement → higher in the old than in the young (per the book).

45-137.r: Daily protein → moderately active adult woman about 45-46 g; adult man about 56 g; lactating mother about 70 g.

45-139.r: Wrong: 'milk has no B vitamins' – it has thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, cobalamin, folate. True: vitamin A lack → dry skin; scurvy → joint pain; thiamine lack → heart failure.

45-140.r: Mother's milk lacks iron; early milk (colostrum) is rich in protein and antibodies, giving passive immunity.

45-141.r: Breast-fed baby (vs bottle-fed) → less obese, resists disease better (mother's antibodies), gets more vitamins and protein; abnormal height growth is not a trait.

45-142.r: Milk (about 87% water) → gives calcium and potassium besides proteins and carbohydrates; only trace iron.

45-143.r: Milk → poor source of vitamin C; rich in protein, vitamin A, B vitamins, carbohydrate, calcium, potassium.

45-144.r: Starch → polysaccharide of many glucose units joined by glycosidic bonds; energy store of green plants.

45-145.r: Wrong: 'both give colour with iodine' – starch turns blue-black, cellulose gives no colour. Both are plant polymers of glucose; cellulose forms plant cell walls.

45-146.r: Malnutrition → results from overnutrition, undernutrition and imbalanced nutrition → all three.

45-147.r: Correct: fatty acids needed in diet; normal diet (2200-2400 calories) has about 75 g fat; essential fatty acid lack causes disease. Wrong: body cannot make any fatty acids.

45-148.r: Linseed → its oil is a very good source of omega-3 fatty acid, which helps prevent fat deposits in blood vessels.

45-149.r: Richest alpha-linolenic acid (18-carbon omega-3, plant type) → flaxseed; also canola, soybean and walnut oil.

45-150.r: A true: vitamins are needed in tiny amounts (micronutrients) for health. R false: white blood cells, not vitamins, destroy harmful bacteria.

45-151.r: A false: glycine, serine, tyrosine are non-essential (made in the body). R true: essential amino acids cannot be made; of 20 amino acids, 10 essential, 10 non-essential.

45-152.r: Complete proteins (all essential amino acids) → milk, egg, soybean (also meat, fish, yogurt); rice lacks some → book gives no single answer (*).

45-153.r: Best source of all essential amino acids → egg, which has the highest Biological Value (BV).

45-154.r: Fat below the skin → insulating layer that prevents heat loss; also an energy store and shock protection.

45-155.r: Most calories per gram → fats (about 9.3 kcal) vs carbohydrates or proteins (about 4.0 kcal).

45-156.r: Maximum energy in metabolism → fats (9.3 kcal per g); proteins and carbohydrates give about 4.0 kcal per g.

45-157.r: Diet group giving maximum energy → carbohydrate, fat and protein.

45-158.r: About 80% of living (organic) material in most organisms → protein; overall, water is the most abundant substance.

45-159.r: Cook in oil, not vanaspati ghee → oils have unsaturated (poly- and monounsaturated) fats that lower blood cholesterol and heart risk.

45-160.r: Sunflower oil → good edible oil because rich in unsaturated fatty acids (mainly linoleic acid): A and R true, R explains A.

45-161.r: For heart patients → sunflower oil: mono- and polyunsaturated fats, low saturated fat, more vitamin E than other vegetable oils.

45-162.r: A true: unsaturated fats are more reactive. R false: unsaturated fats have double bonds; single-bond compounds are more stable.

45-163.r: Fish is healthier than other meat → polyunsaturated fatty acids that lower LDL (bad) cholesterol and heart-disease and stroke risk.

45-164.r: Trans fat is harmful because it lowers HDL ('good' cholesterol); low HDL raises heart-disease risk.

45-165.r: 'No trans-fat' label → no hydrogenated oils, no animal fats/oils, safer for the heart (trans fats raise LDL, lower HDL) → all three correct.

45-166.r: Cholesterol → a sterol (steroid family), a fatty alcohol in animal fat; part of animal cell membranes; abnormal levels → blocked arteries.

45-169.r: Triglyceride → a fat: ester of glycerol + three fatty acids; main body fat; high levels → obesity, high blood pressure.

45-170.r: Wrong pair: Mustard oil – lubricant (mustard oil is not used as a lubricant). Correct: mineral oil–petroleum, vegetable fats–phytosterol, animal fats–cholesterol.

46-001.r: Mammals respire by lungs (take O2 into blood, release CO2).

46-002.r: Nitrogen → same amount in inhaled and exhaled air; oxygen falls, CO2 and water vapour rise in exhaled air.

46-003.r: Oxygen route in the body → lungs → blood → tissues.

46-004.r: Gas exchange in lungs → alveoli, wrapped in capillaries: O2 into blood, CO2 into the air.

46-005.r: Less oxygen in blood (hypoxemia) → breathing rate increases (shortness of breath).

46-006.r: Carbon monoxide → binds haemoglobin as carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO), cutting the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity (hypoxia).
